r1_dissolve_1.principle: The hidden assumption is that each token starts out knowing only itself, so before attention can link a key to its value it must first learn a "previous-token" circuit. Hard-wiring the predecessor into every position (embedding of x_t plus a separate embedding of x_{t-1}) turns mqar and hop (0.20 and 0.10, near chance) into position-free content lookups: the blank, whose predecessor is the query, matches the position whose predecessor is that key and reads off its own token. One layer does one hop and two layers do f(f(x)). These lookups never use absolute positions, so they should also hold at 2x length, and RoPE is kept so copy stays at 1.00 in-distribution.

r1_dissolve_2.principle: The hidden assumption is that a sequence state is a decaying or gated real-valued sum, which can only approximate parity and loses it beyond the trained length (best parity is 0.45 in-distribution but 0.05 at 2x). Parity is really a sum mod 2, which is just a rotation by pi per 1-bit. Adding a few unit-modulus phase channels (a cumulative sum of learned per-token angles, read out as cos/sin) gives a running state whose size never decays, so it stays exact at any length. These features are added to the RoPE transformer's embeddings, so everything that already works is kept.

r1_count_1.principle: Learned token-driven counters: every position's rotary phase is a cumulative sum of per-token learned angles, kept separately for queries and keys (plus a residual phase readout), so attention can match "count of blanks since the separator" against "count of symbols" (copy), find the previous token (mqar/hop), and read off a mod-2 phase (parity). Because a match means two counters are equal, it holds at any length, which targets the near-zero 2x scores (copy 1.00/0.00 and parity 0.45/0.00 for the RoPE transformer).

r1_count_2.principle: Hard-wired predecessor binding: every attention layer computes its queries, keys and values from the concatenation [h_t, h_{t-1}], so "the value whose predecessor equals the query" is a single attention step. mqar then needs one layer and hop (f(f(x))) needs two chained layers, which addresses the measured failure to form an induction circuit in 3000 steps (mqar ID 0.20, hop ID 0.10 at best).

r1_transfer_1.principle: Linked-list pointer chasing from classical data structures. Each cell stores its own token embedding as its address and its successor's embedding as its pointer. One shared content-addressed dereference is applied twice, starting from the previous token (r1 = *x, r2 = **x). Addresses and pointers live in the same embedding space, so the read can be repeated and never uses absolute positions. This targets the failed lookup capabilities, mqar (0.20/0.12) and hop (0.10/0.00), including at 2x length. What maps: pointer = successor embedding, dereference = softmax match on address. What does not map: addresses are not unique (repeated symbols blur the read), so a learned successor-type key term and a position-parity bias stand in for a "valid cell" bit, and there is no write or allocate.

r1_transfer_2.principle: NMR spin precession with re-aligning RF pulses. Each token rotates a bank of complex spins by a learned per-token angle, and a learned per-token pulse pulls each spin back toward a reference phase (this shrinks the magnitude but keeps the angle exact). Attention compares two positions by spin interference instead of by token index. A 1-bit rotation of pi then gives an exact parity sign at any length, which targets parity (0.45/0.05). Spins re-aligned at the marker or separator support "j-th token after segment start" matching for copy at unseen lengths, which targets copy at 2x (best 0.30). What maps: precession angle = token, RF pulse = reset gate, echo/interference = attention score. What does not map: there is no physical dephasing, the rates are learned, and the reset is soft and must be found by training.

r0_blind_1.principle: Count each position from the most recent delimiter (task marker or separator) and feed that count to attention only as a fixed rotary phase. Copy's source-to-target alignment then becomes an exact relative-identity match (delta = 0). Recall and hop stay purely content-addressed, so the usual failure of absolute or sequence-relative positions at 2x length should disappear. A cumulative phase channel with binary-saturating phases supplies parity.

r0_blind_2.principle: Use a token-space pointer machine. One weight-tied lookup ("find the position whose previous token equals my pointer, read its token") is iterated, and each step re-embeds the retrieved token distribution as the next query. The operation itself contains no lengths and its state stays near one-hot, so recall (1 hop), hop (2 hops) and copy (1 hop plus a delimiter-relative positional kernel) should hold at 2x length. Saturating phases supply parity.

r0_blind_3.principle: Replace every positional and counting quantity with learned gated integer counters, n_t = (1 - reset(x_t)) * n_{t-1} + inc(x_t), whose per-token gates saturate to exact 0/1 and are read out only through fixed-frequency rotations. The model discovers its own event-relative clocks for rotary attention (copy alignment, odd/even key-value slots) and its own bit-counters mod 2 (parity). These stay exact integers at any length, which should fix the drift of fixed or absolute position codes beyond the training length.

r2_crossA_1.principle: Put a running token-driven phase (cumsum of learned per-token angles, as in r1_dissolve_2) into the one embedding space that r1_transfer_1's shared successor-dereference reads, and drop every transformer block: the content match still gives mqar and hop, the blank's own unit-modulus phase gives exact parity at any length (r1_transfer_1 scores 0.00/0.07 on parity), and slow symbol-driven and blank-driven phase counters let the same dereference match the j-th blank to the j-th symbol, which targets copy at 2x (best 0.52).

r2_crossA_2.principle: Use one phase-augmented embedding (token plus a running cumsum of learned per-token angles) as the shared address space for both the two-hop successor dereference and a single RoPE attention block, which replaces r1_transfer_1's two blocks. The dereference keeps mqar and hop at 1.00, the phase the dereference and attention read gives r1_transfer_1 the parity it lacks (0.00/0.07), and one block keeps copy in-distribution, so the result is simpler than either parent.

r2_dissolve_1.principle: The hidden assumption is that attention knows a position only by its distance from the query (absolute index, RoPE offset, or spin phase). Copy needs an offset of n+1, and at 2x length that offset was never trained, so the best model scores 0.06 on copy at 2x. Dropping that assumption, each head gives every position two learned token-driven counts (one for the query side, one for the key side, e.g. "blanks seen" and "symbols seen") and scores keys by a kernel on the count difference, -beta*(c_q - c_k)^2. "Blank j reads symbol j" is then a match at difference 0 whatever n is. The rest of r1_transfer_1 (pointer chasing, RoPE blocks) is left untouched, so mqar and hop are kept.

r2_dissolve_2.principle: The hidden assumption is that a position's state must be a weighted average or sum of vectors (attention in r1_transfer_1, which scores 0.00/0.07 on parity). Parity, like any finite-state question, is really the word problem of a finite group, so the state should be a group element: every token applies its own learned orthogonal matrix exp(A_x - A_x^T) to a bank of unit vectors. Products of rotations never decay, and a learned rotation by pi on bit 1 stays exact at any length. This state is fed only into the input of the first block, while pointer chasing still reads the raw embeddings, so mqar and hop are kept.
